findings.claim: Nobody in your audience ever looked at the button that completes the order on the redesign.
findings.evidence: On the review step, “Confirm purchase” sits about 180 px below the fold. Of the 9 people who got that far, 0 looked at it. On your current checkout the same button was seen by 9 of 9, after 2.3 s on average.

findings.claim: A $9.95 service fee only appears after the card is entered, and 4 of 9 people left within 5 seconds of seeing it.
findings.evidence: The fee holds the eye for 610 ms the first time and is returned to 2.4 times — the most re-read thing in the test. The total changes from $129.00 to $147.95 between the two steps.

findings.claim: The sale banner takes the first look in 9 of 10 people, about 1.3 s before they look at any form field.
findings.evidence: It holds 3.1 s of attention against 1.2 s on the button beneath it, and nobody used the code: it costs attention without earning anything.

findings.claim: The payment button says “Place order” but only moves to a review step, and 3 of 11 people stopped there believing they had bought the boots.
findings.evidence: All three look for a confirmation on the next screen, then stop. They end with no order placed — a failure, not someone choosing to leave.

findings.claim: On your current checkout, 2 of 11 people gave up at the cart after re-reading the shipping line.
findings.evidence: Both were price-led shoppers; $8.95 shipping on a $129.00 order was read twice before they left. Reported for balance: the current checkout is the better version, not a perfect one.

findings.claim: 2 of 24 people could not be simulated to the end, and are excluded from both figures.
findings.evidence: Our own browser automation timed out on the card field (one person on each version) after one retry. This is a weakness of the simulation, never evidence against your checkout.
